title: Camus
summary: Camus started from “the absurd” — the collision between the human hunger for meaning and clarity and a silent, indifferent world. His answer is not despair but revolt: to live fully and lucidly, without pretending that a final answer has been found, and to choose life, solidarity and love of the world again and again. “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
onEmotions: Camus did not build a theory of emotions, but his philosophy is very much about feelings: wonder, weariness, the longing for unity, the love of life. He believed that awareness of the absurd often begins not with a thought but with a feeling — a sudden “why?”, a weariness with mechanical routine. He valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to see your feelings honestly, without comforting illusions but also without despair. And he insisted on a passion for life: the sun, the sea, the body, friendship and solidarity were not trifles for Camus but the very heart of what makes life worth living.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a natural response to a world that gives no guarantees. Camus called “the absurd” the collision between the human hunger for clarity and the silence of the world: we want to know that everything will be all right, and the world does not answer. Camus did not suggest pretending there is an answer. He criticized attempts to escape uncertainty into ready-made consolations — the “leap” into a system that explains everything. Instead he proposed “lucidity” (lucidité): seeing uncertainty honestly and still living fully, here and now. From this point of view, anxiety is not an error of the mind but the voice of your hunger for meaning, and it tells you how much life matters to you. There is no need to suppress it; you can admit that there are no guarantees — and return to what is here right now: your breath, the light, your work, people.
anxiety.practice: Name one thing that is definitely here right now: a sound, a light, a sensation. Let the uncertainty of the future sit beside you without cancelling the present.

fear.text: Fear is a legitimate feeling, and Camus knew it from experience: illness, war, underground work in the Resistance. In The Plague the city is sealed off, the epidemic is unpredictable, and fear becomes part of everyday life. But the novel’s hero, Dr. Rieux, does not pretend to be fearless: he simply keeps doing his job. He says it is not a matter of heroism but of decency — of each person doing their work. Camus shows that courage is not the absence of fear but the ability to act alongside it, and not alone but together with others. From this point of view, there is no need to be ashamed of fear. You can acknowledge it and ask yourself what “work of your own,” however small, is within your reach right now.
fear.practice: What is one small piece of “your own work” you can do today — not instead of the fear, but together with it?

sadness.text: Sadness is part of life, and Camus did not see it as an enemy. He is called the philosopher of sun and sea, but he knew that light and shadow cannot be separated. A lucid view of life, for Camus, includes its sorrow too: there is no need to turn away either from the beauty of the world or from its pain. In his early collection of essays, Betwixt and Between, he wrote that there is no love of life without despair about life — meaning that the intensity of feeling alive and its sadness grow from the same root. From this point of view, sadness is not a defeat but part of lucidity: you are seeing life as it is, in all its fragility. And that is exactly why you can love it even more. Sadness does not cancel the joy of living — it deepens it.
sadness.practice: Look at what is saddening you right now and ask: “What love of life does this sadness reveal in me?”

quote.text: There is no sun without shadow, and it is essential to know the night.
quote.author: Albert Camus

grief.text: Grief is a deep pain, and Camus does not offer to explain or justify it. For him, death is part of the absurd: it has no “reasonable” explanation that would make a loss fair. But his answer is not resignation to meaninglessness; it is revolt: the inner “no, it should not be like this” is a legitimate response in which love of life can be heard. In The Plague, Dr. Rieux loses his wife and his friend, and still stays with people, to bear witness and to remember. In the unfinished novel The First Man, the hero stands at the grave of the father he never knew, killed in the war, and suddenly realizes that his father was younger than he is now — and he is flooded with tenderness. From this point of view, grief is a form of faithfulness: by remembering and loving, we keep the bond alive.
grief.practice: If you wish, call up one vivid, concrete memory of whoever or whatever you have lost. Let it simply stay with you for a while.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and Camus understood this well. The hero of The Stranger, Meursault, lives as if apart from shared rituals and expectations, and society never forgives him for being different. But Camus did not stop at estrangement. In The Rebel he arrived at an important idea: each of us experiences the absurd alone, but revolt against injustice and meaninglessness is what unites people. When one person says “no” to suffering, they say it for others too. From this point of view, your loneliness is not proof that you are a stranger but an experience known to a great many people, and through it you can recognize “your own.” Loneliness then becomes not a wall but a bridge to people who feel something similar.
loneliness.practice: Think of someone — a living person or the author of a book — who seems to have felt what you feel. What would you say to them?

anger.text: Anger is a strong and legitimate feeling. For Camus, the central concept is “revolt” (révolte). A rebel, he wrote, is someone who says “no,” but in refusing he does not renounce: his “no” also contains a “yes” — the affirmation of a limit and of values that must not be violated. A slave who refuses to obey affirms that there is something in him that deserves respect. From this point of view, your anger may be pointing to such a value. But Camus also warned of something else: a revolt that loses its sense of “measure” and starts to justify any cruelty betrays itself. Genuine revolt keeps its respect for the human being — including the opponent. You can accept anger as an honest “no” and ask what “yes” stands behind it.
anger.practice: Complete the sentence: “My anger says ‘no’ to …, and ‘yes’ to …”

shame.text: Shame is heavy, and it is almost always tied to other people’s expectations. Camus wrote little about shame directly, but in The Stranger he showed how society judges Meursault not so much for what he did as for not crying at his mother’s funeral — that is, for not having the feelings expected of him. Camus himself later explained that his hero is condemned because he “doesn’t play the game.” From Camus’s point of view, one could say that many of our shames are a fear of not matching the ritual, someone else’s script of the “right” feelings. Lucidity (lucidité) helps separate the two: where I really violated something important, and where I simply didn’t match an expectation. Your feelings do not have to look “the way they’re supposed to.”
shame.practice: Ask yourself: “Am I ashamed because I did something bad — or because I didn’t match someone else’s script?”

guilt.text: Guilt is a heavy feeling, and Camus thought about it deeply. In The Fall (1956), the former lawyer Clamence discovers guilt in himself and turns it into endless self-accusation, which at the same time becomes a way of judging everyone around him. Camus shows that this kind of guilt is a closed circle that fixes nothing and makes no one better. The Plague shows another path. Tarrou says that each of us is in one way or another implicated in the evil of the world — and that is why it is worth trying at least not to add to it, and to stand on the side of those who suffer. From this point of view, guilt can be turned not into self-punishment but into care: what can I do right now to make things a little better?
guilt.practice: Replace the question “How guilty am I?” with “What is one thing I can do right now to make things a little better?” Write down the answer.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, but it is very human. Camus hardly wrote about it directly, but from the standpoint of his philosophy one could say that envy often feeds on the hope that somewhere, for someone, life is “solved” — full of meaning, well arranged, clear — while mine is not. Camus, however, saw the absurd as the common condition of all people: no one has received a final answer from the world, even if it looks that way from outside. The figures in The Myth of Sisyphus matter not because of what they have but because of how lucidly and fully they live what is theirs. Envy can soften when you remember that you see only the surface of another person’s life, and that your own “rock” is yours alone. And in the way you carry it there is a truth of your own that no one can take from you.
envy.practice: What in someone else’s life seems “solved” to you? Ask yourself honestly: does anyone actually have a final answer?

emptiness.text: Emptiness is a very hard state, and Camus knew it from the inside. In the early essay “Death in the Soul” he described how, alone and without money in a foreign city, he felt utterly estranged — everything around him seemed to have lost its meaning. Then, in Italy, the light, the hills and simple life gave him back his sense of the world. For Camus, such moments are an awakening of consciousness, not a verdict. In The Myth of Sisyphus he came to the idea that life does not need a meaning given in advance to be worth living — on the contrary, it can be lived all the more fully without one. From this point of view, emptiness is the moment when the familiar stage sets have fallen, and behind them life itself gradually shows through: light, the body, people.
emptiness.practice: Choose one simple sensation available right now — light, a taste, a sound — and live it fully for a minute without asking “what for?”

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural response to a world that does not explain itself. Camus believed this is not a personal malfunction but the basic human situation: we long for unity, clarity, an understandable meaning, and the world answers with silence. That is the absurd. Camus suggested not looking for a hasty way out — neither in despair nor in a ready-made system that explains everything — but learning to live inside this tension while keeping your “lucidity.” From this point of view, confusion is an honest admission that you don’t know everything, and such an admission takes courage. It is no reason to stop: you can act without final answers, relying on the little that is already clear now.
confusion.practice: Divide a page into two parts: “What I don’t know” and “What is still clear to me.” Even one line in the second column is already something to stand on.

quote.text: The absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.
quote.author: Albert Camus

fatigue.text: Tiredness is real, and Camus perhaps understood it like no one else. His central image is Sisyphus, who rolls his rock up the mountain again and again, and again and again it rolls back down. But what interests Camus most is not the climb but the moment when Sisyphus walks back down to the foot of the mountain: this is the “hour of consciousness,” a pause in which he sees his situation clearly. Camus does not demand heroism or urge you to “push harder.” He invites you to look at your burden honestly and find your own truth in it. We must imagine Sisyphus happy not because the rock is light but because Sisyphus himself owns his attitude toward it. From this point of view, the pause, the descent, the breather are a legitimate and important part of the way.
fatigue.practice: Where in your day is your own “walk down the mountain” — a minute between tasks? Today, try to live it consciously, doing nothing.

boredom.text: Everyone knows boredom, and Camus saw in it the beginning of philosophy. In The Myth of Sisyphus he describes how one day the familiar stage sets collapse: rising, streetcar, four hours in the office, lunch, streetcar, four hours of work, dinner, sleep — and so on, day after day. And suddenly the question “why?” arises. For Camus, that is where everything begins: weariness with a mechanical life awakens consciousness. After that, a person either returns to the old rut or wakes up for good. Camus proposed the second path — not necessarily changing your life abruptly, but starting to see it clearly, noticing what automatism had hidden. From this point of view, boredom is not empty time but a chance to wake up.
boredom.practice: Take one habitual action — your commute, washing the dishes — and do it today as if for the first time.

joy.text: Joy is at the very center of Camus’s philosophy, although he is often thought of as gloomy. In the early essays of Nuptials he writes about Tipasa, about sun, sea, the smell of wormwood, about the happiness of a body that simply lives. For Camus, a lucid understanding of the absurd does not cancel happiness — on the contrary, the two are inseparable: happiness does not need guarantees of eternity to be real. Joy for him is not naivety or an escape from the truth but faithfulness to life itself. From this point of view, rejoicing while knowing the difficulties of the world is also a form of revolt. Joy does not need to be postponed, hidden in shame or justified: it is a legitimate response to the fact that we are alive and the world around us is beautiful.
joy.practice: Find one thing right now that delights your body — warmth, light, a taste, movement — and stay with it for a minute, doing nothing else.

quote.text: Happiness and the absurd are two sons of the same earth. They are inseparable.
quote.author: Albert Camus

love.text: For Camus, love and tenderness are among the highest values, alongside friendship and solidarity. His philosophy of the absurd is not cold at all: it is full of love for the world, for people, for the body, for the sea. One of the brightest episodes in The Plague is the night swim of Dr. Rieux and Tarrou: in the midst of the epidemic, two people find friendship and peace for an hour. For Camus, love does not need eternity to be real: it is precious here and now, in concrete gestures and encounters. From this point of view, tenderness is not weakness but one of the clearest forms of faithfulness to life. You can accept it wholly, without demanding guarantees from it and without fearing its fragility.
love.practice: Recall one concrete moment of tenderness — your own or someone else’s. What made it real at that very moment?

gratitude.text: Gratitude in Camus is above all gratitude to the world: to the sun, the sea, the body, simple joys. He grew up poor in Algeria and later wrote that poverty was never a misfortune for him, because the sun shone on it. After receiving the Nobel Prize, he wrote a letter to his schoolteacher, Louis Germain, admitting that without the hand he held out to a poor child, none of this would have happened. From this point of view, gratitude does not contradict lucidity: the world does not promise meaning, but it gives light, people, moments. Gratitude is a form of love for life as it is, without demands and without conditions.
gratitude.practice: Think of someone who once changed your life, perhaps without knowing it. What would you say to them now?

hope.text: Hope is a complicated subject for Camus, and it is important to understand him correctly. In The Myth of Sisyphus he was suspicious of the kind of hope that draws us away from the present — toward “later,” toward a meaning that will come from somewhere outside and justify everything. He believed such hope can rob us of today. But this is not a sermon of hopelessness. Camus believed in human beings and in solidarity, in the idea that revolt against evil makes sense. The Plague ends with Rieux’s thought that there are more things to admire in people than to despise. From this point of view, hope is not waiting for rescue but an inner strength that lives here and now, in you.
hope.practice: Remember the last time you got through something hard. What was your “invincible summer” then — what held you up?

quote.text: In the depths of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer.
quote.author: Albert Camus

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is one of Camus’s own key words. In The Myth of Sisyphus he speaks of the human “nostalgia” for unity, for clarity, for a world in which we would be “at home.” The absurd is precisely the meeting of this longing with the silence of the world. Camus does not call it a mistake: the longing for unity, in his words, expresses the essential impulse of the human drama. He himself longed all his life for the Algeria of his childhood, for the sun and sea of the Mediterranean. But his answer was not to live only in the past but to carry his love for it into the present. From this point of view, nostalgia is a sign of your deep attachment to the world, and you can accept it with tenderness.
nostalgia.practice: What from the past is calling you now — a place, a feeling, people? Where in today is there even a small glimmer of it?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it right now,” and there is nothing shameful in it. In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to see your situation honestly, without looking away. He called any attempt to slip out of lucid presence in your own life an “evasion” (esquive). From this point of view, one could say that a craving promises a quick way out — out of tension, out of boredom, out of a question with no answer: “do this and it will get easier.” Camus did not condemn people for this thirst for relief: he understood too well how hard it is to live without guarantees. But he considered the living present, seen clearly, to be our greatest wealth. Lucidity here doesn’t require heroism. It means seeing the wave of desire as a wave — it rises, peaks and subsides — and remaining yourself, here, with your body, the light and the people around you.
craving.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and simply watch the craving like the weather: stronger, weaker, changing. At the end, notice what it has become.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure, and Camus never measured people by their purity. His heroes are not saints but people who keep struggling inside a difficult situation. In The Myth of Sisyphus he spoke of the freedom of the absurd man: not a promise that everything will become easy, but the ability to see your life clearly and not hand it over entirely to any power — whether an idea, a fear or a habit. One could say that getting out of a long-standing cycle resembles the way Camus understood revolt: not one great victory, but a daily, modest “no” to what narrows life and “yes” to what widens it. And Camus also insisted that revolt is never a solitary affair: it connects people who recognize a shared struggle in one another. There are always others nearby walking a similar path.
addiction.practice: If you feel like it, think about people walking a similar path — for example, a mutual-help group. Write down what you would want them to understand about you.

hangover.text: A hangover is a hard morning: the body aches, anxiety and shame rise up, there are gaps in your memory. None of this makes you a bad person. Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to look at things directly, without prettifying them and without blowing them up into a catastrophe. From this point of view, one could say that morning shame often offers two traps: pretending that nothing happened, or passing a final verdict on yourself. Camus trusted neither comforting illusions nor despair — both lead away from real life. Lucidity is simpler and gentler: admit that it was hard, calmly find out what you don’t remember if you need to, and return to the simple things Camus loved so much — air, water, light. The body he wrote about with such tenderness needs care right now, not punishment.
hangover.practice: Step outside or go to a window for a minute and feel the air on your face. Tell yourself: “Today I look at this clearly — and without a verdict.”

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, and Camus, who loved life with his whole body, would not have belittled it. In Nuptials he described moments when the boundary between a person and the world seems to disappear: sun, sea, the scent of herbs — and complete agreement with life. For him, such moments were not an illusion but a truth about how generous the world can be. But Camus also valued “lucidity”: joy does not need a promise that it will last forever, and it does not require the whole world to confirm that from now on everything will be different. From this point of view, euphoria can be lived fully — as a gift of this hour, without turning it into an oath to the future. Then even the comedown, if it comes, will not cancel what was.
euphoria.practice: Notice one sensation of this high — in your body, in the way you see, in sounds — and keep it as a gift of today, without promising yourself it will always be like this.

crash.text: A sharp comedown after a high can be very hard: yesterday the world was shining, and today it is gray and cramped. This is not your fault. In The Rebel, Camus thought a great deal about the hunger for “all or nothing”: when a person wants the absolute, everything ordinary starts to look like nothing. Against this he set “measure” — not dull moderation, but the ability to love life as it is: neither shining forever nor empty. From this point of view, a comedown is often intensified by comparison: after the flash, an ordinary day looks gray, although it is simply ordinary. Camus did not reproach people for their longing for the absolute — he considered it deeply human. But he reminded us that between “all” and “nothing” lies almost all of our real life: bread, conversation, a walk, work, the sun.
crash.practice: Name three ordinary things in today that are neither “everything” nor “nothing,” but are still here: a cup of tea, a phone call, the light in the window.

panic.text: Panic is a wave of terror, when your heart pounds and it seems that something irreversible is about to happen. It is genuinely frightening, and you are not exaggerating anything. From the age of seventeen, Camus lived with tuberculosis and knew firsthand what it means to be afraid for your own body and your breath. His philosophy is largely about how to stay in the present when the mind is painting catastrophes. For Camus, what is most certain is not reasoning but what can be felt: in Nuptials the body itself knows the world — warm stone, sun, sea water. From this point of view, there is no need to argue with your thoughts during panic. You can return to what is certainly here: the ground under your feet, the objects around you, the air. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Touch something solid — a table, a wall, the floor — and say to yourself: “This is here.” Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and name five objects around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — when the questions “what is it all for?” and of our own finitude rise up — is one of the hardest experiences there is. Camus knew this question from the inside and did not brush it aside. But his answer is unequivocal: life is worth living even if the world offers no ready-made meaning — and perhaps all the more fully for that. From awareness of the absurd, Camus drew three consequences: revolt, freedom and passion. Revolt is the refusal to give up and the resolve to live with open eyes. Freedom is living without waiting for permission from above. Passion is the fullness of experiencing each day. From this point of view, dread before the abyss is not the end of thought but its beginning: the moment when you see life at its full height. Camus believed that a person can stand before this and still love the sun, people and their day.
dread.practice: Write down one thing you love about today, however small: a taste, a voice, the light. Camus considered such things not trifles but the heart of life.

fomo.text: Almost everyone knows the fear of missing out: it seems that life somewhere out there is brighter, and you are late. In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus wrote that what matters for the absurd man is not to live better but to live more. But he meant not the number of places and events but the fullness of presence: feeling your own life as clearly and keenly as possible. Endless comparison with other people’s lives, by contrast, draws you out of your own day into an imaginary one. Camus loved the concrete: this beach, this morning, this conversation with a friend. For him, the grandeur of life was not somewhere else but here, under this sun. From this point of view, the fear of missing out is not a verdict on your life but an invitation to return to it: the most important thing not to miss is happening where you are right now.
fomo.practice: Describe three details of your “here and now” that appear in no feed: a smell, a sound, the light in the room.

quote.text: Real generosity toward the future lies in giving all to the present.
quote.author: Albert Camus

sleepless.text: Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts are exhausting, and there is nothing strange about everything seeming heavier at night. At the end of The Rebel, Camus speaks of “thought at the meridian” — clear, Mediterranean, on a human scale — as opposed to thought that runs off into extremes and absolutes. One could say that night thoughts are often the opposite of noonday ones: in the dark, when nothing can be done, the mind inflates problems to cosmic proportions, and every question demands a final answer right now. Camus valued lucidity, but lucidity is not endless brooding; it is a calm gaze that comes most easily in daylight. From this point of view, you don’t have to believe your nighttime conclusions. They can be put off until morning, when the world is once again on your scale.
sleepless.practice: Tell the night thought: “I’ll come back to you in daylight.” Then shift your attention to the warmth of the blanket and a slow exhale.

betrayal.text: Betrayal is a deep wound, and your pain and anger are justified. In The Rebel, Camus wrote that revolt begins with a sense of a limit: there is a line that must not be crossed. Betrayal is exactly such a crossing, and your inner “this is not okay” is not touchiness but the affirmation of a value: loyalty, honesty, respect. Camus held friendship and solidarity very high; in The Plague, Dr. Rieux and Tarrou hold on to each other in the midst of the epidemic, and this loyalty is one of the few things the calamity cannot take away. From this point of view, one person’s betrayal does not refute these values themselves. It hurts precisely because they are yours. And they are still alive — in other people and in you.
betrayal.practice: Write down the value this betrayal violated. Then write down one person with whom this value is still alive for you.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and there is nothing shameful in it. Camus hardly wrote about jealousy directly, but from the standpoint of his thought it can be understood as a special form of the longing for clarity. We want to know for sure: what the other person feels, where they are, whether they will choose us tomorrow. And another person, like the world in Camus, gives no final guarantees. Camus called the absurd the collision of our hunger for clarity with the silence of the world; in jealousy this collision takes place inside love. Camus suggested neither pretending that there are guarantees nor giving up love. He valued love as a living presence here and now. From this point of view, you can acknowledge your anxiety without submitting to it entirely, and return to what is really there between you today.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: “What do I know for sure right now — and what am I filling in?” Write the answers as two short lists.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is heavy, and it almost always has a real cause. In The Rebel, Camus drew a subtle distinction between revolt and ressentiment — a hidden, corrosive grievance. Drawing on the philosopher Max Scheler, he described ressentiment as a self-poisoning: a feeling that stews for a long time in powerlessness, in a closed space, and turns against the person themselves. Revolt, by contrast, affirms: there is something valuable in me, and I am defending it. Camus did not demand that you forget or forgive. But he showed that from the same wound not only bitterness but also dignity can grow. From this point of view, your resentment can be recognized as legitimate — and gradually turned from poison into clear knowledge of your own worth and of what you will not allow again.
resentment.practice: Complete the sentence: “This resentment is protecting in me …” Perhaps there is a value behind it that deserves to be acknowledged.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is a sharp pain, and it should not be rushed or be a source of shame. In The Plague, Camus describes how a city under quarantine separates lovers: those who ended up on different sides of the walls live in a true “exile” — going over memories, counting the days, not knowing when the separation will end. Camus writes about this pain with enormous compassion and without reproach. And he shows how people gradually learn to live inside it: not cancelling love, but finding ways to fill today — with work, friendship, care for others. From Camus’s point of view, love, even lost love, is not a mistake but one of the best things that can happen to a person. It was real, and how much it hurts speaks of its strength.
heartbreak.practice: Do one thing today that fills the day not with thoughts of the breakup but with life: a short walk, a call to a friend, something useful.

impostor.text: The feeling that “I’m about to be found out” is very common, and it most often visits conscientious people. Camus, who spent many years in the theater, devoted a whole chapter of The Myth of Sisyphus to the actor. In a single evening the actor lives someone else’s life, knowing perfectly well that he is not Hamlet or a king — and yet he plays in earnest, giving himself wholly to the role. For Camus this is not deception but one of the images of human life itself: the world does not issue us a certificate proving we rightfully occupy our place. All of us, in some sense, play roles we have chosen or that have fallen to us. From this point of view, impostor syndrome is not an exposure but a lucid view of a shared condition. And a role played in earnest is already work honestly done.
impostor.practice: Write: “I play this role in earnest — and that is enough.” Then write one thing you have already done honestly in it.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is a very heavy state, and the inner critic can sound like undeniable truth. But its verdict is not the truth about you. All his life Camus argued with systems that claim final knowledge about human beings and pass verdicts in their name. From the standpoint of his thought, one could say that the inner critic works the same way: it gathers everything worst and passes it off as the complete portrait. Camus, however, saw in every person something that deserves respect — his whole idea of revolt rests on this. So you can rebel against the critic too: not arguing with its every word to the point of exhaustion, but saying “no” to its very role as judge. You are more than what it accuses you of — and you have every right to be on your own side.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one of the critic’s phrases, and beneath it: “I do not accept this judge’s role.” Then write one deed or quality you respect in yourself.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is an agonizing feeling, and it often honestly reflects reality: some things do not depend on us. Camus did not deny this. In The Plague the townspeople cannot stop the epidemic, and no one knows when it will end. But the novel’s characters find what to do inside this helplessness. Grand, a modest clerk, takes on keeping the statistics for the sanitary squads and does it carefully and honestly, and the narrator suggests that he, an inconspicuous man with a good heart, be considered the hero of the book. From this point of view, you need not demand of yourself that you change everything; you can look for your own small, concrete task. Camus believed that such modest participation is already a revolt against powerlessness, and that together people are capable of more than they are alone.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small thing that is within your power today. Do it as carefully as Grand kept his records.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a familiar and painful state, and it almost never comes down to laziness. Often behind it is a fear that the result won’t live up to expectations, or a sense that the task is huge and pointless. In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus offers an unexpected perspective: the meaning of labor is not that the rock should stay at the top forever. Sisyphus knows the rock will roll down, and still he takes hold of it again. For Camus, what is valuable is the effort itself, the climb itself, not the final result. From this point of view, there is no need to wait for certainty that everything will turn out perfectly, or for inspiration that will make the task easy. You can simply put your hands on the rock — begin with the first small movement, without demanding that it be complete.
procrastination.practice: Do the first two minutes of the task — no more. Think not about the summit, only about the first push of the rock.

quote.text: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.
quote.author: Albert Camus

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a deep experience, and Camus knew it personally. He was born and raised in Algeria and loved its sun and sea, but he had to live and work in France; longing for his native land runs through all his work. His last collection of stories is called Exile and the Kingdom (1957): for him, losing one’s place and finding it are always close together. Camus did not suggest forgetting what was lost. He showed that a person can carry their native land within — in memory, in a love of light, in habits — and at the same time gradually find their “kingdom” where they are now: in work, in friendship, in a new landscape. From this point of view, your longing is not weakness but faithfulness to what you love.
uprooted.practice: Recall one thing from home that you carry with you: a taste, a word, a habit. Find a way today to bring it briefly to life in your new place.

overload.text: Overload, noise and the endless feed are exhausting, and this is not a weakness of yours. Camus never knew social media, but all his life he set simple, dense things against the bustle: sun on the skin, the sea, a conversation with a friend, honest work. In The Myth of Sisyphus he admitted that he cannot know the meaning of the world as a whole — but he can feel his own heart and touch the world close at hand. From this point of view, one could say that the feed promises knowledge of everything at once but gives not a single real touch. Camus valued “lucidity,” but lucidity is not a quantity of information; it is a quality of presence. Being tired of noise is the normal reaction of a living person who is starved of the real. Sometimes the best answer is not to learn even more but to feel one single thing.
overload.practice: Put the screen aside for two minutes and choose one physical sensation — the taste of water, the wind, the warmth of your palms. Let that be enough for now.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real is strange and often frightening, and it is hard to talk about. Camus described something similar. In The Myth of Sisyphus he writes about moments when the world suddenly becomes foreign and “dense”: a familiar landscape loses the meaning we had lent it, and the world slips away, becoming itself again. He also mentions the stranger who sometimes meets us in the mirror. For Camus this is not madness but a moment of sudden clarity, when the usual veil falls away. But he did not leave a person in this estrangement: his answer is to return to the world through the body and the senses, through sun, water, touch, living conversation. From this point of view, the world has not disappeared — it has only become unfamiliar for a while.
unreality.practice: Touch water — wash your hands or face — and describe the sensation to yourself: the temperature, the flow, the drops. Let the world answer your body.

awe.text: Awe before something vast and beautiful is one of the experiences Camus held most dear. His early essays, Nuptials (1938), are almost a hymn to this feeling: the ruins of Tipasa among flowers, the sea, the smell of wormwood, a sun in which a person seems to dissolve. Camus called this a “nuptial” with the world — a union in which nothing needs to be explained or earned. There he also writes that he understands what glory is: the right to love without measure. For him, awe does not contradict the clear knowledge that life is finite and the world gives no guarantees. On the contrary, it was precisely knowing this that made him cherish such moments so keenly. From this point of view, awe is not an escape from reality but the fullest encounter with it. You can simply live it through to the end.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, breathing slowly and adding nothing. Then tell yourself: “I saw this.”

relief.text: Relief is a wonderful feeling, and it is worth living fully. The ending of The Plague is one of the most famous descriptions of relief in literature: the epidemic recedes, the city gates open, people rejoice and dance in the streets, those who were separated find each other again. Camus describes this joy with enormous tenderness and makes no attempt to mute it. Dr. Rieux, the narrator, decides to write down what was lived through, to bear witness for those who suffered and to the fact that there is more in people to admire than to despise. One could say that relief in Camus is not forgetting but grateful lucidity: the hard time was real, and the fact that it has passed is real too. Allow yourself both.
relief.practice: Write in one sentence what has become easier, and in another what helped you hold on. Let both be acknowledged.

calm.text: Calm and peace are precious, and Camus knew their worth. In the essay “Return to Tipasa” he describes how, after the hard years of the war, he comes back to the ruins by the sea and finds there the silence and light that had seemed lost. For Camus, calm is not an escape from the world or indifference, but moments of agreement with it, when there is nothing to achieve or prove. From the standpoint of his thought, one could say that such moments give a person back the strength to live, work and care for others again. Calm is not a luxury or idleness but part of the same faithfulness to life as revolt. It needs no justification. You can simply be in it, like being by the sea on a clear day.
calm.practice: Sit for a couple of minutes listening to the quietest sound around you. Don’t try to achieve anything — just be where you are.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful, living state, and Camus knew it as a writer and a man of the theater. In The Myth of Sisyphus he devoted a chapter to creation and called the creator the most absurd of men — in a good sense: he creates without any guarantee that what he makes will be eternal or understood, and still gives himself wholly to the work. To create, for Camus, is to live doubly: to see the world anew and more vividly and to give it form. He believed art should not run away from reality — it brings us back to it, to people, to light, to our shared fate. From this point of view, inspiration is not a whim but a special fullness of presence. There is no need to hold on to it by force: you can simply follow it today.
inspiration.practice: Write down one phrase, image or melody that has come to you now. Don’t judge it — just give it a place on paper.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling few people admit to, but almost everyone knows it. Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — an honest, unembellished look at oneself — so simply admitting such a feeling is already in his spirit. In the novel The Fall, the narrator Clamence dissects with merciless irony his own vanity and his secret pleasure in feeling superior to others; Camus shows that such impulses exist in many people who consider themselves perfectly decent. From Camus’s point of view, one could say that schadenfreude is often born of a sense that you alone are pushing your rock uphill, and someone else’s failure proves for a moment that others have it hard too. But behind this lies an important truth: we are all in the same boat. The absurd is shared, and another person’s failure can become not a reason to feel superior but a reminder of solidarity.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Where in my life right now is the rock that made me want someone else to struggle too?” Write down the answer.

contempt.text: Contempt arises when someone seems petty, dishonest or cruel to you, and sometimes there are real reasons for it. Camus knew this feeling and was attentive to it. In The Rebel he wrote that genuine revolt defends human dignity — including the dignity of the person it is directed against; a revolt that begins to despise people loses its “measure” and betrays itself. And at the end of The Plague, Dr. Rieux, having lived through the epidemic and seen both cowardice and baseness, comes to a simple conclusion about people. From Camus’s point of view, one could say that contempt is a “no” said to a whole person, whereas it is more honest to say “no” to a specific act. You can see another’s weakness clearly and still not deny them the fate you share.
contempt.practice: Divide a page into “what exactly in this person’s act I do not accept” and “what we nevertheless have in common.”

quote.text: …there are more things to admire in men than to despise.
quote.author: Albert Camus

disgust.text: Disgust — with people, with a situation, sometimes with yourself — can be sudden and strong. Camus described similar moments in The Myth of Sisyphus: suddenly the familiar world becomes foreign, people seem mechanical, their gestures devoid of meaning. He mentioned the “nausea” Sartre wrote about and considered this feeling one of the ways a person encounters the absurd. Importantly, Camus did not stop at disgust. He saw it as a moment of awakening: mechanical life has cracked, and you have seen it from the outside. After that a choice is possible — not to turn away from the world but to return to it with clear eyes. So Dr. Rieux in The Plague sees in people both filth and weakness, and still keeps coming to them. Disgust is neither a verdict on the world nor a verdict on you.
disgust.practice: Name one concrete thing that disgusts you. Then name one small thing near you that doesn’t disgust you at all right now.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: when you have been wronged, it feels as if a balance inside has been upset, and you want to restore it. Camus took this feeling seriously. In “Reflections on the Guillotine” he wrote that the ancient law of retaliation, “an eye for an eye,” is rooted in nature and instinct, not in law — that is, it is a natural impulse but a poor basis for action. In The Rebel he showed how revolt against injustice, once it forgets “measure,” begins to commit new injustice of its own. From Camus’s point of view, behind revenge there is usually a right “no”: you cannot treat me like this. That “no” is worth keeping and respecting. But it can be expressed differently — by defending your boundary, naming what happened out loud, refusing to put up with it any longer — without becoming the one who hurt you.
revenge.practice: Complete: “I was hurt, and my ‘no’ means that …” Then: “I can defend this boundary without causing harm, like this: …”

anger_at_loved.text: Being angry with the people closest to you — a partner, parents, children — is very human, and the shame after an outburst shows how much they matter to you. In Camus, revolt is always double: in saying “no,” a person at the same time says “yes” to the value they are defending. With loved ones this is especially clear. Anger usually says “no” not to the whole person but to what has become unbearable: exhaustion, misunderstanding, a recurring hurt. And the “yes” in it is to the relationship itself, in which you want to be heard. Camus insisted on “measure”: genuine revolt does not destroy what it arose for. From this point of view, you need not be ashamed of the anger itself; you can ask what “yes” stands behind it — and take care that its form does not wound those you love. Anger expressed in words rather than blows is also revolt, only with measure.
anger_at_loved.practice: Complete two sentences: “My anger says ‘no’ to …” and “… and ‘yes’ to what I want in our relationship.”

ambivalence.text: To love someone close to you and at the same time be unable to stand them is not a contradiction of character but the ordinary truth of closeness. One of Camus’s first books is called Betwixt and Between (in French, “The Wrong Side and the Right Side”), and one of its essays is “Between Yes and No.” There he writes about his mother: silent, almost deaf, distant — and infinitely dear. His love for her was woven of tenderness and estrangement at once, and he did not try to choose one. Camus was generally wary of attempts to reduce life to a single clear formula. He proposed “lucidity” — keeping both sides in view, the wrong side and the right side. From this point of view, mixed feelings are not an error to be urgently corrected. They are honest knowledge about a person who matters to you so much that they stir everything at once.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page in half: “the wrong side” and “the right side.” In each half write one feeling toward this person, without crossing any out.

guilty_relief.text: Relief you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, a departure, even after the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time — is a very common and almost always hidden feeling. Camus showed it at the end of The Plague: the epidemic recedes, the city rejoices, people embrace in the streets — and in the same crowd walk those who have lost someone. The narrator condemns neither the joy nor the grief: they simply exist side by side. For Camus, honesty about your own feelings matters more than matching what you are “supposed” to feel; The Stranger is in many ways a novel about how society demands the correct emotions. From this point of view, relief does not cancel love. It speaks of how long you carried the weight, and of the fact that life goes on in you. Love and relief can both be true at once.
guilty_relief.practice: Write one sentence that holds both feelings: “I feel lighter, and I still love …” Read it to yourself without justifying anything.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something “should” move you, it is quiet inside. And this quiet is often joined by anxiety: what is wrong with me? Camus devoted one of his most famous novels to this — The Stranger. Meursault does not cry at his mother’s funeral, and the court judges him partly for that. In the preface to the American edition, Camus wrote that Meursault is condemned because he does not play the game: he refuses to lie, that is, to say more than he feels. From Camus’s point of view, one could say that indifference does not always mean heartlessness. Sometimes feelings come later; sometimes numbness protects us from something too strong. Honestly admitting “right now I don’t feel what is expected of me” is already a form of “lucidity.” Your inner state does not have to match other people’s expectations.
indifference.practice: Note what you actually feel right now, even if it is “almost nothing” or “tiredness.” Write it down without the words “should” and “normal.”

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your usual role — is familiar to many. Camus described how it arises in The Myth of Sisyphus: rising, streetcar, work, lunch, work again, sleep — day after day, until one day the question “why?” arises. He called this the moment when “the stage sets collapse” and considered it not a breakdown but an awakening. In The Plague, the journalist Rambert, trapped in the epidemic-stricken city, tries with all his might to get out to the woman he loves, and Dr. Rieux does not condemn him: Camus considered the wish for happiness legitimate. What to choose — to stay or to leave — is for each person to decide, and Camus gave no ready-made recipes. From this point of view, the wish to escape is a signal that you have once again asked about the meaning of your everyday life. It is a valuable question, and it does not need an immediate answer.
escape.practice: Write down: “What exactly do I want to escape from?” and “What would I like to come to?” Just look at these answers without deciding anything.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “wrong” can be very strong and confusing. Camus saw the human being above all as a hunger — for clarity, unity, fullness of life. He called it a “nostalgia” for unity and considered it an inseparable part of us. The absurd, for Camus, arises where this hunger meets a world that does not answer it the way we want. Forbidden attraction is a very vivid case of such a collision: the desire is strong, and circumstances say “no.” Camus warned against two escapes: the “leap” into self-condemnation and the illusion that a single desire can answer everything. From Camus’s point of view, one could say that seeing your desire clearly means neither obeying it nor being ashamed of it. You can simply ask honestly what fullness of life it is speaking of.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write not about the other person but about yourself: “Around them I feel …” What quality of life is it that I long for?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people, of their gaze and their judgment, can be exhausting. Camus understood the power of other people’s judgment well. Clamence, the hero of The Fall, says there is no need to wait for the Last Judgment: it takes place every day — we are constantly judging one another. But Camus shows Clamence as a man caught in a trap: he is so afraid of judgment that he himself becomes a perpetual judge. Camus himself sought the opposite — living camaraderie. He loved the theater precisely for the teamwork, where people do something together instead of evaluating one another. From his point of view, one could say that most of the people around you are also afraid of others’ eyes; this fear is part of our shared human fate. If for a moment you see the people you are talking to not as judges but as equally uncertain human beings, the fear won’t disappear, but it will become a little lighter.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, quietly tell yourself: “This person is a little nervous too.” Notice whether anything changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: you don’t know what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. For Camus this is not an accidental misfortune but the basic condition of life. The world gives no guarantees and does not answer our question “how will it all end?” Camus urged us to live “without appeal” — not postponing life until the day when everything finally becomes clear, because that day may never come. He criticized ready-made schemes that promise complete certainty and called the flight into them a “leap” — a renunciation of lucidity for the sake of comfort. But his conclusion is life-affirming: if the future is not guaranteed, the present becomes all the more precious. You can not know what will happen and still live fully today — work, love, notice the sun. The uncertainty remains, but it stops being the only thing you see.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don’t know how this will end. But today I can …” — and finish with one small thing that depends on you.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — has a way of stretching time and taking away the present. Camus described this in detail in The Plague: the sealed city lives in constant waiting — for letters that don’t arrive, for news, for the end of the epidemic. He calls this feeling “exile”: people are home, it seems, yet their thoughts are always somewhere in the future. Some count the days from morning to night; others — like the modest clerk Grand, stubbornly rewriting a single sentence of his book, or the doctors and volunteers — keep doing their work. Camus does not reproach those who wait; he simply shows that waiting is easier when there is something to do in it, here and now. From his point of view, one could say that waiting need not be drowned out, but you don’t have to give it your whole day either. The present hasn’t gone anywhere while you wait.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, choose one small task unrelated to what you are waiting for, and do it completely.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can return again and again. Camus explored this feeling in The Fall. Once, Clamence failed to help a person in danger, and many years later the moment still haunts him. But Camus shows what regret turns into when it is not lived through: Clamence endlessly passes sentence on himself, and on everyone else along the way — he becomes a “judge-penitent.” The book is a warning: perpetual judgment of yourself does not make you better and helps no one. Camus himself valued something else — “lucidity” and action. The past cannot be changed, but you can honestly name what happened and ask what you can do now, in the life you have. Regret, from this point of view, is not a verdict but knowledge of what matters to you.
regret.practice: Write in one sentence what you regret. Then: “This tells me that what matters to me is …” — and one small action in the spirit of that value.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the sharpest forms of love. Camus described it in The Plague: when the city was sealed off, many were cut off from those they loved. He writes that the first thing the plague brought was “exile,” and that those separated lived on memories and imagined conversations, counted the days, reread old letters. Dr. Rieux himself spends this whole time apart from his wife. Camus does not condemn longing or call on us to drown it out; for him it is an honest side of love, which does not cease to exist across distance. But he also shows that people, while longing, went on living and helping one another. From this point of view, longing is not emptiness but the presence of love. You can carry it without giving up your day.
longing.practice: Write this person a short thought or letter, even if you never send it. Then do one thing they would be glad to see in your day.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can be almost unbearable. Camus wrote The Plague as a book about a calamity that falls on everyone and about how people endure it. His heroes are not superheroes. Dr. Rieux, asked what gives him strength, answers simply: not heroism but decency, that is, doing his job. Tarrou explains that in any calamity he wants to be on the side of the victims. Camus does not demand that you save the whole world. He offers what is within everyone’s reach: not looking away, not lying to yourself, and doing the little you can, together with others. His formula from The Rebel — “I rebel — therefore we exist” — says that even sharp pain for the world unites us with people rather than separating us from them.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, real action for this week — to help, support, call someone. And for today, the news can wait an hour.

quote.text: The only means of fighting a plague is common decency.
quote.author: Albert Camus

rejection.text: Rejection hurts, especially when you opened up and heard “no.” Camus knew this firsthand. After The Rebel came out in 1951, many former intellectual friends, including Sartre, turned sharply away from him, and for years he felt like an outsider in Parisian circles. He did not stop writing. From Camus’s point of view, one could say that rejection is one more encounter with a world that does not answer our call the way we would like. He did not promise that an answer would come. But he showed that the value of your “rock” — your work, your love, your way of living — is not determined by whether you were accepted or not. Sisyphus, rejected by the gods, goes on his way, and Camus invites us to imagine him happy.
rejection.practice: Write: “I wasn’t accepted into … But that doesn’t cancel the fact that I …” — and name one thing that remains yours.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned runs deep — sometimes all the way back to childhood. Camus knew such an early loss: his father was killed in the First World War before the boy was a year old, and his mother was silent and distant. He wrote about this in The First Man, his last, unfinished book. His philosophy contains a similar motif: the absurd is felt as “the silence of the world” — as if the universe does not answer. But from this feeling Camus drew not despair but solidarity: since the world is silent, people need one another all the more. His characters find support not in guarantees but in friendship, shared work, simple human tenderness. From this point of view, your fear speaks of a deep need for connection. It cannot be insured, but it can be cultivated — including with the people who are already near you.
abandonment.practice: Name one person you feel at ease with. Send them a few simple words today — for no particular reason.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds deeply: you turn to someone with your whole heart, and the answer is silence or a polite “no.” Camus defined the absurd as the collision of the human call with the silence of the world, and unrequited love is the absurd in miniature. Camus advised neither pretending that an answer will come nor devaluing your call. He proposed a third way — “lucidity”: seeing that there is no answer and still not renouncing what was alive in you. The capacity to love so strongly is, for Camus, one of the things that make up the very fullness of life. From this point of view, your love was not a mistake because it went unanswered. It testifies that you know how to love. That capacity stays with you — and one day it will again find somewhere to go.
unrequited.practice: Write down three things this love revealed in you: what you learned about yourself, about your tenderness, about what matters to you.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply: it feels as though your dignity has been taken away. Camus, who grew up poor in a working-class neighborhood of Algiers, knew what it is to be on the lowest rung. In The Myth of Sisyphus he retells the myth of a man the gods punished with futile labor: forever rolling a rock up a mountain, only for it to roll back down. It is hard to imagine a more humiliating punishment. And yet Camus writes that at the moment when Sisyphus walks back down toward his rock and becomes conscious of his fate, he is superior to his fate — he is stronger than his rock. From this point of view, dignity cannot be taken from outside: it lies in a clear view of what is happening and in refusing to accept that someone else’s disdain determines your worth. Humiliation speaks of the other person’s act, not of who you are.
humiliation.practice: Write: “I was treated this way, but that says something about …, not about me.” Add one thing in which you keep your self-respect.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background of life. In the early essays collected as Nuptials, Camus wrote about the body with rare joy: swimming in the sea, sun on the skin, the life of the Algerian beaches. In the essay “Summer in Algiers” he says that there the body lives and rejoices openly. For Camus, the body is not a picture to be rated but a way of being in the world: through it we feel water, warmth, wind, the tiredness after work. From this point of view, one could say that dissatisfaction with ourselves often arises when we look at the body only from the outside, as an image. Camus offers a view from within: the body is your way to the sun, the sea, embraces and movement. It does not have to be perfect to give you this encounter with the world.
body_shame.practice: For a minute, pay attention not to how your body looks but to what it feels: warmth, support, breath. Name one pleasant sensation.

illness.text: Illness — when the body lets you down — can take away your strength, your plans and your familiar sense of yourself. Camus knew this personally: at seventeen he was diagnosed with tuberculosis. He had to give up football, which he loved, and later the illness closed off a teaching career to him; the attacks returned throughout his life. And yet it was after this that he wrote his sunniest essays — about the sea, light and love of the world. For Camus, lucidity meant not closing your eyes to the body’s fragility and, at the same time, not handing your whole life over to the illness. From his point of view, one could say that even within limitations there remains room for what he valued most: friendship, thought, beauty, small joys. Illness changes your path, but it does not cancel your presence in the world.
illness.practice: Notice one small thing that brings joy or calm today despite how you feel: light, a sound, a taste, the voice of someone dear.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a healthy and well-earned feeling; there is no need to hide it. Camus has an image of this kind of pride. In The Plague, the narrator suggests that the true hero is not some brilliant figure but the modest clerk Grand — for the bit of goodness in his heart and the persistence with which he did his work: keeping the records of the sanitary squads in the evenings after his office job. Camus valued pride not in superiority over others but in honestly accomplished work. His Sisyphus is happy not because the rock has finally stayed at the top but because the struggle toward the summit is his own. From this point of view, your pride is the recognition that you have put yourself into something real. You can enjoy it — calmly, without apologies and without comparing yourself to others.
pride.practice: Write down what you are proud of and one concrete effort it took. Give yourself a minute simply to be glad.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow and tenderness toward the world are intertwined. Camus knew it well. In the essay “Nuptials at Tipasa” he describes Roman ruins by the sea, flooded with sunlight, the smell of herbs, and in this joy one can hear the thought that everything passes. For Camus, love of the world and a clear understanding of its fragility do not contradict each other — on the contrary, they strengthen each other. Melancholy, from this point of view, is neither an illness nor a defeat but a special sensitivity: you see beauty and at the same time know it is fleeting. Camus did not urge us to get rid of this note; he urged us not to turn away from the light in which it sounds. Bright sadness can simply be lived — like a warm evening you don’t try to stop.
melancholy.practice: Find something beautiful and fleeting nearby — light, a cloud, a sound. Look at it for a minute, doing nothing with whatever feeling comes.
